extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (registered patent attorneys and agents), applicants for USPTO registration, and patent-practice counsel advising practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedures, and examples governing registration, ethics, investigations, and sanctions for practitioners who practice before the USPTO (attorneys, agents, and non-practitioners who offer to practice). Includes registration criteria, common misconduct types, procedural time limits, diversion/mitigation, and sanction types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of the Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED is primarily responsible for registering attorneys and agents to practice before the USPTO; developing and administering the registration examination (Patent Bar); investigating allegations of misconduct by practitioners; and administering/overseeing the USPTO Law School Clinic Certification and Patent Pro Bono programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes OED's roles and the scope of its oversight rather than a prescriptive rule, but frames the contexts in which disciplinary standards and processes apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration requirements for practice before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Three factors for registration: (1) scientific and technical qualifications; (2) legal competence demonstrated by passage of the registration examination; and (3) moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: 37 C.F.R. § 11.7 and the General Requirements Bulletin. All three factors must be satisfied for authorization to practice in patent matters (attorneys, agents, limited recognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patent practitioner eligibility and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: New technical criteria (effective Jan 2, 2024) allow applicants with specified degrees (e.g., industrial design, product design, architecture, applied/graphic/fine arts, art teacher education, or equivalent) to qualify as design patent practitioners; must still pass the registration exam and moral character evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon registration, design patent practitioners may practice in design patent matters only. Applicants meeting Category A/B/C scientific criteria who sit for the exam can also practice design patent matters. See OED Design Bar flyer and GRB for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practice before the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the USPTO includes communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the USPTO, consulting with or giving advice in contemplation of filing a patent application (or other document) with the USPTO, and similar activities for trademark matters (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.5(b), 11.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants by a practitioner is permitted. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(1)-(2) and § 11.14 for further detail on who may practice in trademark and other non-patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Artificial Intelligence in practice and certification duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners' use of AI-based tools may implicate ethical duties; 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 imposes duties in connection with submissions before the USPTO, including certifications (formed after reasonable inquiry) as to evidentiary support for factual contentions and the practitioner's signature obligations (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.4(d)(1), 2.193).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance issued Apr 11, 2024 (Federal Register) on use of AI-based tools. Practitioners must ensure that papers submitted are supported by reasonable inquiry and that use of AI does not undercut certification duties. See USPTO AI resources link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary jurisdiction of OED
rubrics_metrics.description: OED disciplinary jurisdiction covers all practitioners engaged in practice before the USPTO (including trademark practitioners, pro hac vice in PTAB, representatives in OED proceedings) and non-practitioners who engage or offer to engage in practice before the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory authority: 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32. Governing regulations include USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101–11.901) and procedural rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19–11.60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance, investigation, and time limits for formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigation begins with receipt of a grievance (a written submission presenting possible grounds for discipline). Time period for filing a formal complaint is 1 year from receipt of the grievance but not later than 10 years from the date of misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-reporting is often considered a mitigating factor. After investigation, the OED Director may terminate with no action, issue a warning, institute formal charges (with Committee on Discipline approval), or enter into a settlement agreement for USPTO Director approval. See 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d) and § 11.22(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee on Discipline (COD) and adjudicative process
rubrics_metrics.description: OED presents investigation results to the COD, which determines if probable cause exists. If probable cause is found, the Solicitor files a formal complaint with a hearing officer; the hearing officer issues an initial decision which may be appealed to the USPTO Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.22, 11.23, 11.32, 11.34, 11.40, 11.54, 11.55. If no appeal is taken, the initial decision becomes the USPTO Director's final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning letters (non-disciplinary disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A warning is neither public nor a disciplinary sanction; the OED Director may conclude an investigation by issuing a warning that contains a statement of facts and identifies the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct relevant to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A warning will not be available if a formal complaint has already been filed with a hearing officer. Citation: 37 C.F.R. § 11.21.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of disciplinary sanctions and reinstatement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions include exclusion from practice before the USPTO (minimum five years), suspension for an appropriate period, reprimand or censure, probation (in lieu of or in addition to other sanctions), and possible conditions on reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion requires petition for reinstatement (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58(a), 11.60(a)); exclusion minimum five years per 37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b). Suspension reinstatement only upon grant of petition after suspension period. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.20 for sanction types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline, interim suspension, and exclusion on consent
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may impose reciprocal discipline based on discipline by a state or federal program/agency (often on documentary record), impose interim suspension based on conviction of a serious crime (then refer to hearing officer for final action), or effect exclusion on consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.24 (reciprocal), 11.25 (interim suspension), 11.27 (exclusion on consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversion Program for practitioners (mitigation pathway)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Diversion Program (formalized as a rule Aug 2023; 37 C.F.R. § 11.30) provides a diversion pilot/formal program for practitioners facing issues such as substance use, depression, anxiety, stress, or other difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program background notes prevalence statistics (ABA/Hazelden study). Guidance available at USPTO Diversion Guidance Document link. Participation can be a mitigating factor in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of client matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect (failure to handle client matters adequately) is a recognized form of misconduct under multiple rules, including 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) (neglect) and 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) (disreputable or gross misconduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presentation highlights that many USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct address neglect and candor. Case example: In re Kroll (D2014-14) involved failure to file an application and poor docket management resulting in a two-year suspension; aggravating factors included prior disciplinary history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to communicate with the client
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to communicate with clients is a listed example of misconduct subject to OED discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such failures can be treated as neglect and may lead to sanctions depending on severity, prior history, and mitigating factors (e.g., self-reporting, participation in diversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lying to or deceiving a client
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly lying to a client is identified as misconduct and can trigger investigation and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of dishonesty are aggravating factors in disciplinary proceedings and may lead to severe sanctions including suspension or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of candor to the USPTO / certification obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must be candid to the USPTO; 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b) requires parties presenting papers to make a certification (after reasonable inquiry) as to evidentiary support for factual contentions and allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of candor is a serious ethics violation; case law and rules (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)) are cited as bases for discipline. Misrepresentations on filings can lead to formal complaints and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest — prohibition and waiver conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not represent a client when there is a concurrent conflict of interest (representation directly adverse to another client or a significant risk representation will be materially limited). See 37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may represent despite a concurrent conflict only if: (1) the practitioner reasonably believes competent and diligent representation to each client is possible; (2) representation is not prohibited by law; (3) it does not involve assertion of a claim by one client against another client represented by the practitioner in the same proceeding; and (4) each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing (37 C.F.R. § 11.107(b)). See also §§ 11.108(f) and 11.504(c). Case In re Radanovic (D2014-29) illustrates sanctions (public reprimand) for conflict-related conduct (representing joint inventors without written agreement and continuing despite dispute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure, candor, and good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have ongoing duties of disclosure, candor, and good faith in dealing with the USPTO and clients; failures in these duties are grounds for discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encompasses duty to disclose material information/relationships and to act in good faith during prosecution and communications. Violations appear throughout cited rules and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee handling and trust account issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Improper handling of fees and trust accounts is listed as a common form of misconduct subject to OED discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust account mismanagement and improper fee practices may result in investigations and a range of sanctions depending on severity and history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent agent privilege — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent agent privilege can protect confidential communications between a client and a registered patent agent when intended to be confidential and made for the purpose of seeking or giving advice about a matter (applies to activities agent is authorized to perform, e.g., preparing/prosecuting patent applications, consulting about filings, drafting specs/claims, drafting amendments/replies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope varies by state/federal case law. Cases discussed: Onyx Therapeutics v. Cipla (D. Del. 2019) (narrow application), In re Queen’s University (Fed. Cir. 2016) (privilege recognized only for activities agents are authorized to perform), In re Silver (Tex. 2018) (Texas Supreme Court ultimately recognized privilege). Application depends on whether communications were reasonably necessary and incident to prosecution; litigation contexts often parse these limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case examples used as sanction/mitigation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected OED case decisions illustrate how rules are applied (e.g., In re Kroll: two-year suspension for posting inventions publicly, failing to file, poor docketing; In re Radanovic: public reprimand for conflict-related conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These case summaries highlight aggravating/mitigating factors (prior history, lack of candor, self-reporting, written agreements) and typical sanctions tied to particular misconduct patterns.
